did_you_know.text: The verse opens by describing the exiles sitting by the rivers of Babylon and weeping as they remember Zion; their national memory is a source of pain and longing.
The “willows” in the verse are willow trees, on which the exiles hung their harps. The image expresses the end of their music and their mourning.
The captors ask the exiles to sing “one of the songs of Zion,” but the request is presented as part of their captivity and mockery: they demand joy from people who have lost their homeland.
The question, “How can we sing the LORD’s song in a foreign land?” expresses the connection between sacred song and the people’s homeland and national circumstances.
The speaker swears never to forget Jerusalem, using especially forceful language: if he does forget her, may his right hand lose its ability to act.
The memory of Jerusalem comes before every other joy: the speaker asks that Jerusalem be “above my highest joy,” meaning at the top of his emotional and national priorities.
The poet asks the LORD to remember the people of Edom, who, according to the verse, called for Jerusalem to be destroyed “down to its foundations”—until it was completely ruined.
Babylon is called “Daughter Babylon, doomed to destruction,” and the verse portrays her future downfall as repayment for what she did to the people speaking.

The final verse uses a disturbing image of children being dashed against the rock. It is the language of a harsh curse of retribution, expressing the depth of the anger and grief after the destruction.
